Two years ago I printed a map of my neighbourhood, pinned it to the kitchen wall and started colouring in every street I walked down. I had lived there for a decade and assumed I knew it well. By the end of the first month I had found a community orchard, a cul-de-sac of houses with blue front doors and a footpath that nobody I asked had ever heard of.
## Slowness is a feature
Walking is slow, and that turns out to be the point. At walking pace you notice the hand-painted sign in the hardware shop window, the tree that flowers a week before all the others, the man who sweeps the pavement outside the launderette every morning at seven. From a car or a bus, all of that blurs into background.
I started keeping a small notebook. Not a journal exactly, just a list of things I would otherwise forget: a street name I found funny, a front garden full of rhubarb, a bench with a plaque for someone who “loved this view”. The list is now forty pages long.
> You do not need to travel far to be somewhere new. You only need to turn left where you usually turn right.
## The streets nobody walks
The hardest streets to finish were not the long ones but the awkward ones: service roads behind supermarkets, a dead end that ran alongside the railway, a private-looking lane that turned out to be a public right of way. Those were also, almost without exception, the most interesting. They are where a neighbourhood keeps the things it does not put on display.
I finished the last street in November, on a wet Sunday afternoon, with nobody there to see it. Then I bought a map of the next neighbourhood over.
